name: Wärtsilä on AI in Maritime: Voyage Optimisation, Predictive Maintenance and Digital Twins
title: Wärtsilä on AI in Maritime: Voyage Optimisation, Predictive Maintenance and Digital Twins
answer: Wärtsilä's site documents its commercial maritime AI, chiefly the Fleet Optimisation Solution for route and fuel efficiency, the Expert Insight predictive-maintenance service combining AI anomaly detection with expert analysis, and digital-twin work on vessel performance. Its most useful single claim is that operators have cut unscheduled maintenance by 25% on average using real-time data, AI diagnostics and human expertise, with 90% of issues resolved remotely and 80% within 24 hours.

sections.body: Wärtsilä, the marine and energy equipment and technology company, publishes these pages on its own website. They comprise insight articles, a white paper page, product pages for lifecycle services, webinar pages and energy-sector commentary. The maritime material is commercial in origin but describes deployed technology and named customer cases, including Carisbrooke Shipping, Brittany Ferries, Livestock Express and the shuttle tanker Aurora Spirit. The energy pages address data centre power and grid balancing rather than transportation AI directly. No publication dates are given beyond the December 2020 Aurora Spirit case and a 2019 adoption date for Carisbrooke.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The maritime pages describe AI applied to vessel efficiency and maintenance. Voyage optimisation uses machine learning on weather forecasts, sea conditions and vessel data to compare routes and recommend the most fuel-efficient option, recalculating continuously to avoid storms, high waves or congested lanes. The Fleet Optimisation Solution supports routing, fuel efficiency and fleet performance. Digital twins replicate a ship's characteristics and systems from design data including computational fluid dynamics simulations, then receive real-time engine, fuel, weather and navigational data to recommend actions such as hull cleaning. Expert Insight combines AI-based anomaly detection with rule-based diagnostics and human experts: the algorithms compare live data against a vessel's unique operating profile, while rules define the boundaries of optimal equipment behaviour from configuration, design recommendations and field experience. Flagged anomalies are investigated by assigned experts who advise crews through an online app. The white paper describes predictive maintenance, data-driven maintenance interval planning and remote issue resolution as proven approaches, with experts filtering weak signals so crews are not flooded with noise. Elsewhere the site argues that 90% of data generated onboard never leaves the deck, and that chartering, still largely manual, may be where machine learning has the deepest impact.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: Carisbrooke Shipping has used the Fleet Optimisation Solution since 2019 and reported fuel savings of 5.7%. Operators have reduced unscheduled maintenance by 25% on average using real-time data, AI diagnostics and human expertise, with 90% of issues resolved remotely and 80% within 24 hours. Estimates cited say 90% of data generated onboard never leaves the deck, and maritime moves 90% of the world's goods. Livestock Express operates 15 livestock carriers. In December 2020 Expert Insight detected abnormal lube oil pressure at a turbocharger inlet on the Aurora Spirit near Stavanger, leading to a bearing replacement guided remotely.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: This is a vendor's account of maritime AI in commercial service rather than a research paper, and its value lies in the operational detail. It shows how voyage optimisation, digital twins and predictive maintenance are actually configured, including the hybrid of machine learning and rule-based diagnostics that keeps false alarms manageable, and the human expert layer that validates findings. The named customer cases and the maintenance and remote-resolution figures give a reader concrete benchmarks for what AI-assisted vessel operations claim to deliver, and the observation that most onboard data never leaves the ship identifies a practical constraint on further deployment.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Transportation

sections.body: The material is published by Wärtsilä to describe and sell its own services, so the performance figures come from the company and its customers rather than independent evaluation. Several pages are webinar or product descriptions with little technical detail, and the energy articles on data centre power and grid balancing sit outside transportation AI. Dates are sparse, and the maritime content does not cover autonomous navigation, regulation or competing systems, so it should be read as one supplier's record rather than a survey of the field.
